title: Altman, Amodei brief UN Security Council on AI as France chairs first CEO-level session
subtitle: The 15-member Council heard directly from OpenAI, Anthropic, Hugging Face, DeepSeek and Moonshot in a session convened by French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: France used its September Security Council presidency to hold a high-level briefing on artificial intelligence and international security on September 23, chaired by Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot. Briefers included Yoshua Bengio, co-chair of the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue. Chinese frontier developers DeepSeek and Moonshot were invited to make statements to the Council.

The mechanism matters as much as the guest list. This is the first time the Security Council has directly hosted the CEOs of leading US and Chinese AI labs together on a shared safety agenda, and it happened in the chamber that authorizes sanctions and peacekeeping — not a General Assembly side event or a G7 lunch. France framed the discussion around systemic risks from misalignment and loss of control over the most advanced systems, drawing on the Bengio-led International AI Safety Report as the shared factual base.

The session lands in the middle of a coordinated push. Altman was expected to argue for international coordination and shared benchmarks for evaluating advanced systems; both OpenAI and Anthropic published safety framework proposals in the days beforehand. It also follows Wednesday's Xi-Trump summit in Washington, which formally launched a US-China AI dialogue track. Together the two events signal that great-power AI diplomacy has moved from op-eds to institutional agendas over the last month.

For learners, the lesson is that AI governance is now doing what climate governance took twenty years to do: forcing the companies building the technology and the states that host them into the same room, on the record. That does not mean binding rules will follow quickly — the Council rarely legislates the frontier — but the moment a topic reaches this venue, national governments start writing their own domestic laws to match. Track those bills, not the New York speeches.
